cards.text: Nehemiah is leading God's people as they rebuild the wall around Jerusalem. About that time, a great outcry goes up from the people and their wives. And friend, this is a whole different kind of trouble.

cards.question: The people and their wives are crying out. Who is this great outcry against?

cards.text: Some families say they have lots of sons and daughters, and they must get grain to eat and stay alive. Friend, I raised six kids who were COOKIE CUTTERS, they never ate one crumb, and I STILL lost sleep.

cards.question: Other families are trying to get grain too. What are they mortgaging to get it?
Those families are trying to get grain during a famine.

cards.text: Still others have borrowed money just to pay the king's tax on their fields and vineyards. That's not a budget, friend, that's one bill paying off another bill.
Then comes the part that hurts most. They say their children are just like their countrymen's children.

cards.question: Yet these parents are subjecting their own sons and daughters to ___.
Some of their daughters are already enslaved. Why can't the parents buy them back?

cards.text: Nehemiah hears every word of it. The outcry, the complaints, all of it.

cards.question: When Nehemiah hears the people's outcry, he stays calm and quiet.

cards.text: Calm? NOPE. Nehemiah gets extremely angry, but he gives it serious thought before he speaks, and friend, angry AND thinking at the same time is a rare combo.

cards.question: After serious thought, Nehemiah rebukes the ___ and officials.
What does Nehemiah say the nobles and officials are doing?

answers.text: Charging interest to their own brothers
Skipping their shifts on the wall
Hiding grain from the king's men

cards.text: So Nehemiah calls a large assembly against them. He tells them they've done their best to buy back Jewish brothers sold to foreigners, and now YOU are selling your own brothers so they can be sold back to us, and friend, that's not a rescue, that's a revolving door.

cards.question: When Nehemiah calls them out, the nobles and officials fire back with excuses.

cards.text: Nehemiah keeps going. "What you are doing is not right."

cards.question: Nehemiah says the nobles and officials should walk in the fear of God. What would that help them avoid?

cards.text: Then Nehemiah says he, his brothers and his servants have been lending the people money and grain too, and he says, "Please, let us stop this usury." Not "you," friend. "US."

cards.question: Next, Nehemiah tells the nobles and officials what to give back to the people. What is it?
Nehemiah wants the people's land and houses given back ___.

cards.text: And not just the land. He wants back the percentage they've been charging on the money, grain, new wine and oil, and friend, that's not an apology, that's a FULL REFUND.

cards.question: The nobles and officials tell Nehemiah they need time to think it over.
The nobles agree to give it all back. To make the promise stick, Nehemiah summons the ___.

cards.text: The nobles and officials say, "We will restore it," and promise to require nothing more. Then Nehemiah has them take an oath that they'll do what they promised.
Then Nehemiah shakes out the folds of his robe. I shake the flour out of my apron every night, friend, but when Nehemiah does it, it MEANS something.

cards.question: Nehemiah shakes out the folds of his robe. What does he say it means?

answers.text: God shaking out every promise breaker

cards.text: The whole assembly says, "Amen," and they praise the LORD.

cards.question: After all the big promises to give everything back, what do the people actually do?

cards.text: Now Nehemiah looks back on his time as governor of Judah. King Artaxerxes appointed him, and he served from the king's twentieth year to his thirty-second year.

cards.question: From the king's twentieth year to his thirty-second, Nehemiah serves as governor for ___ years.
In all those years as governor, what do Nehemiah and his brothers never eat?

answers.text: The food allotted to the governor
The food set aside for the priests
The food sent from the king's palace

cards.text: The governors before him heavily burdened the people, taking bread and wine plus forty shekels of silver, and even their servants oppressed the people. But Nehemiah does not do this.

cards.question: Nehemiah won't burden the people like the governors before him. Why not?

answers.text: Because of his fear of God

cards.text: Instead, he devotes himself to building the wall, and all his servants are gathered there for the work. A boss who skips the perks and shows up to WORK, friend, I would frame that boss and hang him in my bakery.

cards.question: Nehemiah uses his time as governor to buy up land.

cards.text: And Nehemiah's table is PACKED. 150 Jews and officials eat there.

cards.question: Guests from the surrounding nations eat at Nehemiah's table too.

cards.text: Every day, one ox, six choice sheep and some fowl are prepared for him, and every ten days there's an abundance of all kinds of wine. Friend, I fill cookie boxes ALL DAY, and SIX SHEEP A DAY still made me sit down.

cards.question: Even feeding all those people, Nehemiah won't demand the food allotted to the governor. Why not?

answers.text: The people's burden is so heavy
The nobles pay for it all

cards.text: Then Nehemiah turns to God and prays.

cards.question: After everything he's done for the people, what does Nehemiah ask God?

cards.text: And that's where we'll set this one on the cooling rack for now. Trust me, friend, Nehemiah's story is still in the oven.

rule.text: He calls the baker "baker" or "friend," and talks to one baker at a time. Never "my baker," "kids" or "sweetie."

findings.problem: The opening card states a fact from outside the passage (Nehemiah leading the people in rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, Neh 2–4) with no reference. It cites only Nehemiah 5:1.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: "This is a whole different kind of trouble" tells the baker the outcry is not about the outside enemies. That rules out the wrong answers on card 2 (the Samaritan army, the Ashdodites).

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The retelling switches pronouns partway through: "He tells them they've done their best to buy back Jewish brothers" reads as if the nobles did the buying back. Nehemiah says "We have done our best" about his own side (5:8). The card also packs the assembly, the speech and the joke into one long run-on second sentence.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: Card 8 already tells the baker the nobles agree to give it all back and that Nehemiah summons the priests. Card 9 then goes back to tell the agreement again, out of order. That makes it partly a recap.

Three jokes use the same template: "That's not a budget... that's one bill paying off another bill" (stop 1 card 6), "that's not a rescue, that's a revolving door" (stop 1 card 15), and "that's not an apology, that's a FULL REFUND" (stop 2 card 6). It reads as a formula.

rule.text: No formula. His personality fits whatever moment he's in, whether it's a tense moment in a story, a hard teaching or a quick question. There are no joke quotas and no required kinds of jokes.

findings.problem: This is Artaxerxes' first appearance, but the card calls him only "King Artaxerxes" and never says who he is (king of Persia).

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: "I would frame that boss and hang him in my bakery" mixes images. "Frame" can mean setting someone up, and "hang him" about a person reads darkly. A stranger could stumble on it.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The closing line copies the doc's example almost word for word: "And that's where we'll ... for now. Trust me, friend, ..." mirrors "And that's where we'll leave it for now. Trust me, friend, this story's not done."

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: The final card is only the story-continues line and tells no verse, yet it cites Nehemiah 5:19. The docs say every story card cites the verses it tells, and they allow a last card that is just this line, but they don't say what such a card should cite.
findings.question: When the last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line and tells no verse, what should its "verses" field be: the passage's last verse, the whole passage, or something else?
